topics.title: Classes and Inheritance
topics.summary: Model data and behaviour with classes, instance vs class attributes, and reuse code through inheritance.
topics.description:
A **class** is a blueprint; an **object** (instance) is something built from it. Classes bundle data (attributes) and behaviour (methods).

### Defining a class
```python
class Account:
    bank = "PyBank"                 # class attribute, shared

    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        self.owner = owner          # instance attribute
        self.balance = balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        self.balance += amount
```
`self` is the instance and is passed automatically. `__init__` initialises a new object.

### Method kinds
- Instance method: gets `self`.
- `@classmethod`: gets `cls`; often used as alternative constructors (`Date.from_string`).
- `@staticmethod`: no automatic argument; a plain function living in the class namespace.

### Inheritance
`class Savings(Account):` reuses and extends the parent. `super()` calls the parent's version of a method. Python supports **multiple inheritance**; the **MRO** (method resolution order, `Class.__mro__`) decides lookup order using C3 linearisation.

### Encapsulation by convention
`_name` means "internal, please don't touch"; `__name` triggers name mangling to avoid clashes in subclasses. Python has no truly private attributes.

### Composition over inheritance
If the relationship is "has a" rather than "is a", store an object as an attribute instead of inheriting. It is usually more flexible.
keyPoints: __init__ initialises each instance; self is the instance
Class attributes are shared; instance attributes belong to one object
classmethod gets cls, staticmethod gets nothing
super() delegates to the parent class
Prefer composition when the relationship is "has a"
pitfalls: Mutable class attributes shared by all instances
Deep inheritance trees that are hard to follow

examples.title: Inheritance with super()

interview.q: What is the difference between a class attribute and an instance attribute?
interview.a: A class attribute is stored on the class and shared by all instances; an instance attribute is stored on the object and is unique to it.
Method Resolution Order: the order in which Python searches base classes for a method, computed by C3 linearisation and visible via __mro__.
classmethod receives the class as first argument and can create instances; staticmethod receives nothing and is just a namespaced function.

topics.title: Dunder (Magic) Methods
topics.summary: Special double-underscore methods that let your objects work with Python syntax and built-ins.
topics.description:
Methods named `__like_this__` ("dunder" = double underscore) are hooks Python calls for built-in operations. Implementing them makes your objects behave like native types.

### Most useful
| Method | Triggered by |
|---|---|
| `__init__` | `Class(...)` |
| `__repr__` | `repr(obj)`, debugging, REPL |
| `__str__` | `str(obj)`, `print(obj)` |
| `__len__` | `len(obj)` |
| `__getitem__` / `__setitem__` | `obj[key]` |
| `__iter__` / `__next__` | `for x in obj` |
| `__contains__` | `x in obj` |
| `__eq__`, `__lt__` ... | `==`, `<` ... |
| `__add__`, `__mul__` | `+`, `*` |
| `__call__` | `obj()` |
| `__enter__` / `__exit__` | `with obj:` |
| `__hash__` | `hash(obj)`, dict keys |
| `__bool__` | `if obj:` |

### repr vs str
`__repr__` is for developers and should ideally look like valid code; `__str__` is for end users. If only `__repr__` is defined, `print` uses it too, so always write `__repr__` first.

### Equality and hashing
If you define `__eq__` without `__hash__`, instances become unhashable. Objects that compare equal must have equal hashes.

### Operators return NotImplemented
For unsupported operand types return `NotImplemented` (not raise) so Python can try the reflected operation.
pitfalls: Mutating objects used as dict keys

examples.title: A Vector class

interview.a: __str__ gives a readable string for users; __repr__ gives an unambiguous developer representation. print() uses __str__ and falls back to __repr__.
Equal objects must have equal hashes so they work correctly in sets and as dict keys; defining __eq__ alone sets __hash__ to None.

topics.title: Dataclasses
topics.summary: Generate __init__, __repr__ and comparisons automatically for classes that mainly hold data.
topics.description:
`@dataclass` (module `dataclasses`, Python 3.7+) writes the boring methods for you based on **annotated fields**.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Product:
    name: str
    price: float
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
```

You automatically get `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__`.

### Useful options
- `frozen=True`: instances are immutable and hashable.
- `order=True`: adds `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` comparing fields in order.
- `slots=True` (3.10+): less memory, faster attribute access.
- `kw_only=True` (3.10+): all fields must be passed by keyword.

### Field tricks
- `field(default_factory=list)` for mutable defaults (a plain `= []` is rejected).
- `field(repr=False, compare=False)` to hide or exclude a field.
- `__post_init__` runs after `__init__` for validation or derived fields.
- `field(init=False)` for computed fields.

### Helpers
`asdict(obj)`, `astuple(obj)`, `replace(obj, price=5)`, `fields(cls)`.

### Dataclass vs alternatives
`namedtuple` is immutable and tuple-like; plain classes give full control; **Pydantic** models add validation and parsing, which is why FastAPI uses them.
keyPoints: frozen=True makes instances immutable and hashable
asdict() and replace() are handy helpers
pitfalls: Using a mutable default value directly
Forgetting that fields without annotations are ignored
Expecting runtime type validation (there is none)

examples.title: Dataclass in use

interview.a: They remove boilerplate (init, repr, eq) for data-holding classes while remaining normal classes you can extend.

interview.q: How do you give a dataclass field a list default?
interview.a: Use field(default_factory=list); a bare list default would be shared across instances and is rejected.

topics.title: Properties and Encapsulation
topics.summary: Control attribute access with @property getters, setters and computed attributes.
topics.description:
A **property** lets you expose a method as if it were a plain attribute. You can start with a simple public attribute and, later, add validation or computation **without changing the calling code**.

```python
class Temperature:
    def __init__(self, celsius):
        self._celsius = celsius

    @property
    def celsius(self):
        return self._celsius

    @celsius.setter
    def celsius(self, value):
        if value < -273.15:
            raise ValueError("below absolute zero")
        self._celsius = value

    @property
    def fahrenheit(self):          # read-only computed
        return self._celsius * 9 / 5 + 32
```

### Why not getX()/setX()?
Python prefers direct attribute access. Properties give you Java-style control only where you need it.

### Read-only and computed attributes
Define only a getter and assignment raises `AttributeError`. Combine with `functools.cached_property` for expensive values.

### Deleter
`@celsius.deleter` handles `del obj.celsius`.

### Under the hood: descriptors
`property` is implemented with the **descriptor protocol** (`__get__`, `__set__`, `__delete__`). Methods, `classmethod` and `staticmethod` are descriptors too. You rarely write one, but it explains how attribute lookup works.

### Naming conventions
`_x` = internal, `__x` = name-mangled. Use them to signal intent, not to enforce secrecy.

### When to choose a property
Pick a property when an attribute needs validation, must stay consistent with another attribute (like `fahrenheit` derived from `celsius`), or when you want to deprecate a stored field and compute it instead. If the attribute is just data, keep it as a plain public attribute.
keyPoints: @property turns a method into an attribute read
Properties allow changing internals without breaking callers
Descriptors are the mechanism behind property
pitfalls: Naming the backing attribute the same as the property (infinite recursion)
Doing slow work in a property getter without caching

examples.title: Validated property

interview.a: To add validation or computation behind attribute syntax, keeping a stable public interface and avoiding getter/setter boilerplate.
No. A leading underscore is a convention, and double underscore triggers name mangling, but neither prevents access.

topics.title: Abstract Base Classes and Enums
topics.summary: Define interfaces that subclasses must implement, and named constants with Enum.
topics.description:
### Abstract base classes (ABC)
An **ABC** declares an interface: methods that every subclass must implement. A class with unimplemented `@abstractmethod`s cannot be instantiated, so mistakes show up early.

```python
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Shape(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def area(self) -> float: ...
```

Use ABCs when you want an explicit contract and shared base behaviour, for example payment gateways or storage backends. For lighter "duck typing" with static checks, use `typing.Protocol` instead.

### Enums
`Enum` defines a fixed set of named constants. Compared with plain strings or ints they are safer (typos fail), self-documenting and iterable.

```python
from enum import Enum, auto

class Status(Enum):
    ACTIVE = auto()
    BANNED = auto()
```

- Access: `Status.ACTIVE`, `Status["ACTIVE"]`, `Status(1)`.
- `.name` and `.value` give the label and the value.
- `IntEnum` and `StrEnum` (3.11+) behave like ints/strings and are handy for JSON or database values.
- `Flag` supports bitwise combinations of options.

### Where you meet them
Django `TextChoices`, SQLAlchemy `Enum` columns, FastAPI request parameters restricted to a set of values, and state machines in your own code.
keyPoints: Use auto() to generate values and StrEnum for string values
Protocol is the structural alternative to ABC
pitfalls: Using strings as magic constants instead of Enum
Comparing an Enum member to its raw value (Status.ACTIVE == 1 is False for plain Enum)
Instantiating an ABC with missing abstract methods

examples.title: ABC and Enum

interview.q: What does an abstract method do?
interview.a: It forces subclasses to implement it; a class that does not cannot be instantiated.
Enums group related constants, prevent invalid values, support iteration and give readable names in logs and debugging.
